12.title: Fix Your Eyes on Jesus: The Discipline of the Father
12.overview:
Chapter 11 filled the stadium; chapter 12 says: run. Strip off what slows you, keep going, and look at Jesus, who ran the hardest course and sat down at the finish. Then the writer reads the readers’ hardships for them: not a sign that God has left them, but the training a Father gives his children, painful now and fruitful later.

The chapter ends with two mountains. Sinai was fire, darkness and a voice the people begged to stop. The church has come to Mount Zion: the city of God, angels in festival, the assembly of the firstborn, the righteous dead made perfect, and Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel’s. So do not refuse the one speaking, and worship with reverence, because the God of Zion is still a consuming fire.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Run the Race, and Read the Discipline
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Surrounded by so many witnesses to faith, believers should throw off every hindrance and the sin that trips them, and run their race with endurance, keeping their eyes on Jesus, who began and completes our faith. For the joy ahead he endured the cross, scorning its shame, and now reigns at God’s right hand. Considering what he endured from sinners will keep them from losing heart; they have not yet resisted to the point of bloodshed. Their hardships should be understood as a father’s discipline. As Proverbs says, the Lord disciplines those he loves; that is proof that they are his children. Human fathers discipline for a short time as they think best; God disciplines for our good, that we may share his holiness. It is painful at the time, but it produces a peaceful harvest of righteousness in those trained by it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Timescales

Run looking to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him. The Father's discipline is painful for the moment, but later yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Suffering believers wondered whether God had abandoned them.

Now: Hardship received from God's hand is a mark of sonship, not of rejection. Do not make light of it, and do not faint under it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, with so many witnesses around us, let us throw off everything that slows us down, and the sin that so easily trips us, and run with endurance the race marked out for us.

Witnesses. Martys, the people of chapter 11 to whom God bore witness. The stands are full of those who have finished, and their lives prove the course can be completed.

Are they watching us? Some read this as the dead looking on. The word points mainly to testimony, not spectating: they are witnesses to faith more than witnesses of us. Whether they see us Scripture does not say, and it gives no warrant for praying to them.

Weight. Not sin. Bulk. Runners raced stripped of perfectly respectable clothes. Some things are not wrong and must still go because they slow you down. Each runner must name his own.

A textual note. Almost all manuscripts say sin “clings closely” or “easily entangles”. The earliest papyrus has a word meaning “easily distracts”. The majority reading is more likely original, and both are true to experience.

Set before us. Someone else marked the course. You are not responsible for its length or hills, only for staying on it.

On a Tuesday. Is there a hobby, habit or screen that is not sin but keeps you from prayer and people? Put it down.

verseByVerse.quote: looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your eyes on Jesus, who began and completes our faith. For the joy ahead of him he endured the cross, thought nothing of its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of God’s throne.

Looking. Looking away from everything else, including the heroes just listed, to him.

Founder and perfecter. The pioneer at the head of the column (2:10) and the one who brings faith to its end. He is at both ends of the course. The Greek says “the faith”: not only the best example of believing, but the one who starts and finishes it in us.

The joy. He went to the cross not grimly but for a joy beyond it: bringing many sons to glory (2:10). We were the joy set before him.

Despising the shame. Crucifixion was designed to humiliate. He reckoned the disgrace not worth weighing against the joy.

Seated. The finish line. He ran, he finished, he sat down: proof that the course ends.

For worship. The one you are looking at once looked at you, and thought the cross worth it.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Think about him who endured so much hostility from sinners, so that you do not grow weary and lose heart. In your fight against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of bloodshed.

Consider. An accounting word: work out the proportion. The cure for weariness offered is a comparison.

A hard, fair word. They had suffered shame, prison and loss (10:32–34). But no one had died. Exhaustion makes your own trouble fill the horizon; the writer restores the scale.

Against sin. He reframes their persecution as a fight with sin itself, the same contest Jesus was in.

A textual note. Several early manuscripts read “hostility against themselves”: sinners harming themselves by opposing him. The ESV’s “against himself” has wide support and suits the sense better.

On a Tuesday. When you feel you cannot go on, do the sum: what did he endure, and what have you?

verseByVerse.quote: And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you forgotten the encouragement Scripture speaks to you as sons? “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, and do not lose heart when he corrects you, because the Lord disciplines the one he loves and punishes every son he accepts.”

Addresses. Present tense. Proverbs 3:11–12 is God speaking to them now.

My son. Said first, and it governs all that follows. This is spoken inside a family.

Two opposite errors. Shrugging hardship off as meaningless weather, or being flattened by it as if God had turned against you. Most of us lean one way.

What it does not mean. Not that every affliction punishes a particular sin. Chapter 11 was full of people who suffered for being faithful, and Job and the blind man (John 9:3) forbid that conclusion. Paideia is a child’s whole training, of which correction is one part. God is forming, not settling accounts; Christ settled those.

On a Tuesday. In a hard week, ask “What are you teaching me, Father?” rather than “What did I do?”

verseByVerse.quote: It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Endure hardship as discipline: God is treating you as his children. What child is not disciplined by his father? If you are never disciplined, as all his children are, you are not really his children.

Their hardship, read. The shaming and the confiscations are called God’s training.

What it does not mean. Not that the persecutors were right, or that injustice is not injustice. God uses it without approving it (Genesis 50:20).

Illegitimate. A man did not invest in raising another man’s child. The frightening thing is not discipline but its absence. A life God never interrupts or corrects is not a sign of his favour.

The inversion. They looked at their troubles and wondered if they were still his. He says: this is what having a Father looks like.

parallels.desc: as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We had human fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. How much more should we submit to the Father of spirits and live? They disciplined us for a few years as they thought best; he does it for our good, so that we may share his holiness. No discipline is pleasant at the time, but painful; later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness for those trained by it.

Honest about fathers. Human discipline is brief and a matter of judgement, often wrong: in anger, inconsistent, for the wrong things. If your father was harsh, this verse does not ask you to call that love. It points you to a Father who never gets it wrong.

His holiness. The aim is not better behaviour but a share in what God is.

Painful. All of it. Do not tell suffering people to enjoy their trials. It is not meant to feel good.

Trained. The gym word of 5:14. The fruit is not automatic. The same trouble leaves one person bitter and another gentle, depending on whether it was received as training.

On a Tuesday. A man nursing his wife through a long illness said, “I hated every month of it, and I would not give back what God did in me.” That is verse 11.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they should strengthen weak hands and shaky knees and make straight paths, so that the lame are healed rather than disabled. They must pursue peace with everyone and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord, making sure no one falls short of God’s grace, that no bitter root springs up to poison many, and that no one is immoral or careless of holy things like Esau, who sold his birthright for a meal and later found no way back. The writer contrasts two mountains. They have not come to Sinai, with its fire, darkness, storm and a voice so terrifying even Moses trembled. They have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to countless angels, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge of all, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus, mediator of the new covenant, whose blood speaks better than Abel’s. So they must not refuse the one who speaks from heaven. God will shake earth and heaven once more, and only what cannot be shaken will remain. Receiving an unshakable kingdom, they should be thankful and worship God with reverence and awe, for he is a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Mountains

Believers have not come to the terrors of Sinai but to Mount Zion, to Jesus and his sprinkled blood. And our God is still a consuming fire: what has changed is our access, not his nature.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Esau sold his birthright for a single meal.

Now: Watch for anyone falling short of grace, and ask what you could not bear to lose — that shows what your life rests on.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So lift your tired hands and steady your weak knees. Make level paths for your feet, so that the lame leg is not dislocated but healed.

Tired, not rebellious. The words are Isaiah’s to exiles (Isaiah 35:3). This is the writer’s picture of his readers: worn out.

Do something. Lift, strengthen. A weary person has a part to play, and being told so is part of the help.

For the limping one. A rough path is fine for the sound and dangerous for the injured. The question is not what I can manage, but what the weakest person in the church can manage, and whether my way of walking helps or harms them.

Healed. The lame are not written off. The expectation is recovery.

On a Tuesday. Who in your church is limping? A phone call, a lift, a meal can level a path.

verseByVerse.quote: Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.

Everyone. Even the neighbours who plundered them, so far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18). Peace takes two.

Held together. Peace alone becomes appeasement; holiness alone becomes cold separatism. Chase both.

What it does not mean. Not that seeing God depends on your achieved purity. Christ has “perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (10:14). This is the holiness that always accompanies being made holy: no one sees the Lord who has not been made holy by Christ, and no one made holy by Christ fails to pursue holiness. The pursuit is evidence, not payment.

Views. Some Christians teach that a second experience can bring entire sanctification in this life. “Pursue” implies the thing is not yet caught. We run until we see him, and then we will be like him (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch over one another, so that no one falls short of God’s grace, and no bitter root springs up, causes trouble and poisons many.

See to it. The verb behind “overseer”. It is given to the whole church, not only the elders.

No one. The letter keeps scanning the room for the one person slipping away (3:12; 4:1).

Root of bitterness. From Deuteronomy 29:18, where the root is a person whose heart has turned from God. So it is first about one turned heart in a church, and fairly applied to private resentment too.

The sequence. Underground, then a grievance that seems reasonable, then sympathisers, then many people who caught something they did not go looking for.

On a Tuesday. Deal with resentment early, in yourself and gently in others. Roots are easier to pull before they surface.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make sure no one is sexually immoral, or godless like Esau, who sold his rights as firstborn for one meal. You know that afterwards, when he wanted the blessing, he was rejected: he could find no way to undo it, though he sought it with tears.

Not a monster. A hungry man. “Unholy” means common, profane: a person for whom nothing is sacred.

Was Esau immoral? Genesis does not say so, though Jewish tradition later did. More likely only “godless” describes Esau, and immorality is a separate danger.

One meal. Genesis gives no agonising: he ate, drank, rose and went his way (25:34). The readers were not asked to renounce Christ formally; they were offered relief for something they could not see. Esau’s trade is drift with a price on it.

What it does not mean. Not that Esau repented and God refused him. His tears were for the blessing, not for his contempt. “No chance to repent” most likely means no way to reverse the transaction: Isaac could not change his mind (Genesis 27:33–38). Some decisions cannot be undone, and grief afterwards does not restore them.

For the anxious. If you fear you have done this, your sorrow over sin itself is evidence you have not. Esau never had it.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have not come to a mountain that can be touched, to fire, darkness, gloom and storm, to a trumpet blast and a voice so dreadful that those who heard begged for no more words. They could not bear the command that even an animal touching the mountain must be stoned. The sight was so terrifying that Moses said he was trembling with fear.

Untouchable. Sinai’s first feature: you could not touch it on pain of death (Exodus 19:12–13).

Fire without light. Fire, darkness, storm together: deliberately disorienting.

Begging God to stop. “Do not let God speak to us, lest we die” (Exodus 20:19). Offered God’s own voice, a nation asked for it to end.

Even a beast. An ox that strayed across a line it could not understand was killed. Holiness does not make allowance for ignorance.

Moses trembled. The words are not in Exodus; Hebrews draws on Deuteronomy 9:19, where Moses says he was afraid, and on Jewish tradition about Sinai. If the mediator shook, what was it like at the foot of the mountain?

verseByVerse.quote: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to countless angels in joyful assembly, to the church of the firstborn whose names are written in heaven, to God the judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to his sprinkled blood, which speaks a better word than Abel’s.

Have come. Perfect tense: arrived and standing there. Not one day. These people sat in an ordinary room in a hostile city; this is where they really were.

The city. The city Abraham looked for (11:10). He never reached it. They have.

Angels in festival. At Sinai, terror; here, celebration.

Firstborn. Every member an heir, a few verses after Esau sold his birthright.

God the judge. Not softened, even at the feast.

The righteous made perfect. The believing dead, chapter 11 among them, with God now (11:40).

Better than Abel’s. Abel’s blood cried for justice (Genesis 4:10). Christ’s speaks pardon.

For worship. On Sunday, in a small church with a struggling organist, this is where you are. Sing like it.
verseByVerse.note: Abel’s blood cried out for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks of pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not refuse the one who is speaking. If Israel did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, we will certainly not escape if we turn from him who warns from heaven. Then his voice shook the earth; now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”

Is speaking. Present tense, again. God speaks in Scripture now.

Refuse. The same word as “begged” in v. 19: to ask to be excused. You can decline a word without disputing it. Many do it by simply never opening the Bible.

From heaven. Lesser to greater, as at 2:2 and 10:28.

Haggai 2:6. Spoken to men rebuilding a modest temple. It is called a promise, which tells you which side of it the readers are meant to stand.

When? Some apply it to the end of the old order in AD 70. That was a foretaste. But shaking heaven as well as earth points to Christ’s return and the new heavens and earth (2 Peter 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Yet once more” means that what can be shaken, created things, will be removed, so that what cannot be shaken will remain.

From two words. As with “new” in 8:13. “Once more” means one last time, and what survives the last shaking is permanent.

A sifting. The shaking is for something: so that the unshakable may remain. It removes only what was going to fall anyway.

A rehearsal. The readers’ property had already been shaken from their hands, and they found they still had “a better possession and an abiding one” (10:34).

On a Tuesday. You can find out now what your life rests on: notice what you could not bear to lose.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be thankful, and so worship God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

Grateful. The phrase can also mean “let us have grace”. Both fit: grace received produces thanks, and thanks is how grace is held.

Receiving. No one builds or earns this kingdom. It is handed over.

Reverence and awe. The letter has opened the curtain and told the frightened to come boldly. It will not let boldness slide into casualness.

A consuming fire. Deuteronomy 4:24. The God of Zion is the God of Sinai. What has changed is our access, not his nature.

What it does not mean. Not that believers should fear being burned up. For those in Christ, the fire refines and protects (Zechariah 2:5). But anyone who concludes that God has become manageable has misunderstood the cross.

For worship. Our God is a consuming fire: the most frightening sentence in the letter, or the most comforting, depending on which mountain you have come to.

For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven.<sup>26</sup>At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”<sup>27</sup>This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.<sup>28</sup>Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe,<sup>29</sup>for our God is a consuming fire.

13.title: Outside the Camp: The Unchanging Christ
13.overview:
The sermon lands in ordinary life: keep loving each other, welcome strangers, visit prisoners, honour marriage, be content with what you have. This is not a change of subject. People who have come to Mount Zion live this way in their own streets.

At the centre stands verse 8: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” The founding leaders have died; Christ has not changed, so there is nothing newer to chase. Then the letter’s last appeal: Jesus suffered outside the gate, so go out to him, bearing his disgrace, for here we have no lasting city. The Christian’s sacrifices now are praise and practical kindness. The letter closes with a great benediction: the God who raised the great Shepherd works in us what pleases him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter turns to practical life. Brotherly love must continue. Believers should show hospitality to strangers, for some have entertained angels without knowing it, and remember prisoners and the mistreated as if sharing their suffering. Marriage is to be honoured by all and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers. Their lives should be free from the love of money, content with what they have, because God has promised never to leave or forsake them, so they can say with confidence that the Lord is their helper and they need not fear what people can do.
verseByVerse.theology:
Where the Argument Lands

The letter's theology ends in hospitality, prison visiting, marriage and money. Contentment rests on a promise: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Visiting prisoners marked a believer out publicly, and these readers had done it before.

Now: Keep loving, keep welcoming, keep remembering those in prison as though in prison with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep on loving one another as brothers and sisters. Do not forget to welcome strangers into your homes, because some people, by doing so, have entertained angels without knowing it.

Continue. The love is already there. The writer is not telling a cold church to start, but a tired one not to let go.

Love of strangers. Philoxenia, set beside philadelphia: family affection widening to people you do not know. With few safe inns, and travelling preachers depending on it, hospitality was the church’s infrastructure, and in a hostile city it carried risk.

Angels unawares. Abraham at Mamre (Genesis 18), Lot, Gideon, Manoah. Each was being ordinarily kind and did not know what was happening.

What it does not mean. Not a promise that disguised angels regularly knock, or a call to ignore wisdom. The first readers chiefly welcomed travelling Christians and believers in need (3 John 5–8). It is a motive: you never know how much God is doing through a meal.

On a Tuesday. Ask the new family, the student, the widower home for soup. That is how most of the church’s history was made.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham, Lot and others welcomed angels without first knowing who they were.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember those in prison as if you were there with them, and those being ill-treated, since you also have a body.

Remember. Roman prisons did not feed inmates. Remembering meant carrying bread through a door everyone could see you enter, identifying yourself with the prisoner. These readers had done it before (10:34).

As though with them. Not sympathy at a distance. Imagine yourself in the cell.

In the body. Either the body of Christ, so what happens to one happens to all, or your own body, so you are just as vulnerable. Both are true; the second is the more likely sense of the Greek.

Against instinct. A frightened group distances itself from members who are arrested. The letter asks for the opposite.

On a Tuesday. Write to a persecuted Christian, support a prison ministry, or visit someone in hospital who has no other visitors.

verseByVerse.quote: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage should be honoured by everyone, and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

By all. Single people included. Honouring marriage is the whole church’s duty.

Two errors. Some despised marriage as unspiritual (1 Timothy 4:3); others treated it as no limit on desire. The verse honours it and guards it.

Undefiled. Scripture is not embarrassed by sex in marriage. It calls it clean and good, and is glad about it (Proverbs 5:18–19; the Song of Songs). Husband and wife are to give themselves to each other freely (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). Outside the marriage of one man and one woman it belongs nowhere: not adultery, not pornography, not the lustful look (Matthew 5:28).

God will judge. Not only because it harms people, though it does. The matter is between you and God first, whether or not anyone else ever finds out.

Why here? Pressure does not exempt anyone from ordinary temptations. Frightened, exhausted people reach for comfort.

For the fallen. Judgment is real, and so is cleansing. The same letter offers a blood that makes the conscience clean (9:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let love of money rule your life; be content with what you have, because God has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can anyone do to me?”

Silver-loving. The cure for wanting more is not having more but being satisfied with what is in the house.

A sting. They had lost property (10:34). Going back would likely have got some of it returned.

The promise. God’s words to Joshua (Joshua 1:5). The Greek piles up negatives: never, no, never. The remedy offered for love of money is not a better financial position, but God himself.

What it does not mean. Not that saving, earning or planning is wrong (Proverbs 6:6–8). Love of money is the problem, not money.

Psalm 118:6. God speaks; the church answers with Scripture. The question is defiant, not naive. People can do a great deal, and these readers had the empty houses to prove it. But with God beside you, what does it finally amount to?

On a Tuesday. When you scroll through what you cannot afford, say the promise aloud: he will never leave me.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They should remember the leaders who taught them God’s word, consider the outcome of their lives and imitate their faith, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever. They must not be carried away by strange teachings, especially about ritual foods; the heart is strengthened by grace. Christians have an altar from which the old priesthood has no right to eat. Just as the bodies of sacrificial animals were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make his people holy by his blood. So believers should go out to him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace he bore, because here they have no lasting city but seek the one to come. Through him they are to offer God a continual sacrifice of praise and not neglect to do good and share, which pleases God. They should obey and submit to their leaders, who keep watch over their souls and must give account, so that their work is a joy and not a burden. And they should pray for the writer, who has a clear conscience and hopes to be restored to them soon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Outside the Camp

Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp. Go to him there, bearing his reproach, and offer the sacrifices that please God: praise, doing good and sharing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For these readers the camp was home — temple, synagogue, festivals and family table.

Now: Leaving what is not lasting is not homelessness; it is going to where he is.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember your leaders who spoke God’s word to you. Think about how their lives turned out, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever.

Their credential. Not office or title, but what came out of their mouths: the word of God.

The outcome. The “exit”, how it ended. Doctrine is tested over a lifetime. Anyone can hold a view at forty; what a man is at the close is the evidence. The founders had probably died, some perhaps for the faith.

Imitate their faith. Not their manner or gifts. The one thing you can copy.

The same. The answer to a particular grief: the leaders are gone, and Christ is not. Yesterday when you first heard; today in this trouble; for ever past every pastor you will have.

Does it mean the miracles continue? Continuationist Christians argue that an unchanging Christ will act as he acted. But the verse is about who Christ is: his character, saving work and word. The signs that confirmed the apostles’ message belonged to that first generation (2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). By the other argument, he would still be walking in Galilee. That view is held here charitably.

For worship. Your church changes, your health changes, your world changes. He does not.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be carried off by all kinds of strange teaching. It is good for the heart to be made strong by grace, not by rules about food, which have never helped those who live by them.

Diverse and strange. Many-coloured and foreign. Christ is the same; teachings vary. Their very variety is evidence against them.

Foods. Ceremonial meals or food laws, part of the old system. Are Christians bound by them? No. Jesus “declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19); “everything created by God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4). Those who keep such rules from conscience are not to be despised (Romans 14:1–3). The danger is trusting them to steady the heart.

Why they attract. Rules are measurable. You know if you kept them, and they give a sense of progress grace never does.

Not benefited. An empirical verdict. Look at those devoted to it: has it done them good?

On a Tuesday. The modern version is any spiritual programme, diet or routine you trust to make you right with God. Keep the routine if it helps; rest your heart on grace.

verseByVerse.quote: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have an altar from which those who still serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. The high priest carried the blood of the sin offering into the sanctuary, but the animals’ bodies were burned outside the camp. So Jesus too suffered outside the city gate, to make his people holy by his own blood.

An altar? After twelve chapters dismantling altars, the writer claims one. Roman Catholic teaching takes it as the altar of the Mass. But this letter insists Christ was offered once for all, never repeated (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:12–14). Others take it as the Lord’s Supper. The more likely reading is that the altar is the cross: we eat from it by sharing in Christ’s sacrifice by faith, which the Supper signs. Those who cling to the shadow have no share in the substance. You cannot hold both.

Outside the camp. On the Day of Atonement the sin offering’s body was burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27), the one sacrifice no priest ate.

Outside the gate. Golgotha was outside Jerusalem’s wall. Not an accident of Roman practice but the ritual fulfilled.

For worship. The one thrown out, where the refuse went, is the one who makes his people holy. If you have ever felt on the wrong side of a boundary, he went there first.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So let us go out to him outside the camp, and bear the disgrace he bore. For here we have no city that lasts; we are looking for the city that is to come.

The whole appeal. Thirteen chapters, and this is what they ask: come out.

What the camp was. For Jewish Christians, not paganism but home: temple, synagogue, festivals, family table, and the legal shelter Judaism had under Rome. The pull backwards was not towards sin but towards belonging.

To him. Not out into nothing. He is no longer inside. If you want him, go where he is.

What it does not mean. Not a call to leave every church or tradition, or to despise the Jewish people. It is a call to leave any system that offers acceptance with God apart from Christ, and to accept the disgrace of belonging to him.

No lasting city. Jerusalem would be rubble within a few years. What you would keep by staying was never permanent.

On a Tuesday. Being known as a Christian in your family, office or club may cost you standing. That is where he is.

verseByVerse.quote: Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Jesus, then, let us continually offer God a sacrifice of praise, the words of lips that confess his name. And do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, because God is pleased with sacrifices like these.

What goes on our altar. Two offerings, both within anyone’s reach.

Through him. Even praise goes up through our priest. A struggling Christian’s worship is accepted for the same reason as his forgiveness.

Continually. The sacrifice for sin was once for all; this one never stops.

Fruit of lips. From Hosea 14:2.

Sharing. Practical kindness is called a sacrifice beside worship. A meal cooked, money given, a spare room offered please God.

What it does not mean. Not that these sacrifices atone. They are thank-offerings from people already forgiven.

On a Tuesday. Your quiet help is not the lesser, less spiritual part of your faith. It is on the altar.

verseByVerse.quote: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obey your leaders and defer to them. They keep watch over your souls as people who must give an account. Let them do this with joy, not groaning, for that would do you no good.

The ground. Not seniority, but responsibility. They stay awake over you like sentries, and will be audited by God. That should make anyone think twice before wanting the job.

How far? The leaders meant are those who speak God’s word (v. 7), followed as they lead by it. Where they command what Scripture forbids, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). The Bereans checked even an apostle (Acts 17:11). Elders must not domineer (1 Peter 5:3).

What it does not mean. Not a licence to control, silence or exploit. A leader who does so should be confronted and, if he will not listen, brought before the other elders (1 Timothy 5:19–20). A believer harmed may seek help and, if need be, leave. Abuse that is a crime must be reported to the authorities.

Joy or groaning. A congregation that exhausts its leaders hurts itself: a discouraged man watches less well.

On a Tuesday. Send your pastor a note of thanks this week. Most never hear one.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray for us. We are sure our conscience is clear, and we want to live honourably in every way. I especially ask you to pray, so that I may be brought back to you soon.

Two-way traffic. After thirteen chapters of authority, he asks for help. A teacher who can only give is in fellowship with no one.

A clear conscience. Perhaps someone had questioned his motives. He states it and moves on, often the right way to handle an accusation you cannot disprove.

Restored. Separated by something unnamed, illness, prison or distance, he misses these particular people.

Nameless. One of the most learned writers in the New Testament, and no one recorded his name. Fitting for a man who told his readers to seek a city to come. The work mattered, not his name.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who teach you, by name.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer closes with a blessing: may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the eternal covenant, equip them with everything good to do his will, working in them what pleases him through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever. He urges them to bear with his brief word of exhortation, reports that Timothy has been released and may come with him, sends greetings to all their leaders and believers, passes on greetings from those from Italy, and ends with grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Works in Us

The God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, equips his people and works in them what pleases him. What he requires, he supplies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The writer calls his letter a “word of exhortation”, a sermon sent to people he knows and misses.

Now: After its hardest warnings, the letter ends with grace for all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the God of peace, who brought our Lord Jesus back from the dead, the great Shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with every good thing to do his will. May he work in us what pleases him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

God of peace. Apt for a church under strain, with leaders groaning.

Brought again from the dead. The only explicit mention of the resurrection in Hebrews. It has been assumed throughout: a seated priest is a living one.

The great Shepherd. From Isaiah 63:11, where God brought up Moses, the shepherd of his flock, from the sea. A greater Shepherd, brought up from death: a new exodus.

By the blood. The ground of his rising. The covenant his blood sealed could not have a dead mediator. And it is eternal, unlike the old one that was vanishing (8:13).

Equip. To mend, as nets are mended or bones set.

Working in us. The hinge. What he requires, he supplies (Philippians 2:13). That is why the letter’s demands are not crushing.

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “working in you” and “every good work”. The differences are small; the ESV’s “in us” has good early support and includes the writer with his readers.

For worship. Pray this benediction over someone you love, by name.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and sisters, please bear with this word of encouragement; I have written briefly. Our brother Timothy has been released, and if he comes soon I will see you with him. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send greetings. Grace be with you all.

A sermon sent. “Word of exhortation” is the phrase for a synagogue sermon (Acts 13:15). That explains the missing greeting, the spoken rhythms and the argument by quotation.

Briefly. Perhaps dry humour after thirteen chapters; more likely honest: he could see how much more there was to say.

Timothy. The only name in the letter, released presumably from prison. It places the writer near Paul’s circle and settles nothing more.

Who wrote it? Some early Christians thought Paul. But the style differs, and the writer received the gospel from those who heard the Lord (2:3), which Paul said he did not (Galatians 1:12). Apollos, Barnabas, Luke and Priscilla have been proposed. The likeliest answer is a gifted teacher in the apostolic circle whose name God did not preserve. The letter’s authority rests on the God who speaks in it.

From Italy. Either Italians abroad greeting home, or believers in Italy greeting elsewhere. Both are possible.

All. Twice. A letter with warnings that have frightened readers for centuries ends by including everyone, and with grace.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy had evidently been in prison. “Those who come from Italy” may be Italians abroad sending greetings home, or believers in Italy itself.
